power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Sex moderates the relationship between the Dark Triad and trait aggression
table.research_questions:
1) What is the association between Dark Triad traits and trait aggression?

2) Does sex moderate the association between Dark Triad traits and trait aggression? Prediction 1: 

The core of the Dark Triad will be positively associated with all components of aggression (physical, verbal, anger, hostility) in both men and women. Psychopathy will uniquely predict higher levels of physical and verbal aggression, whereas narcissism will uniquely predict lower levels of hostility.

Prediction 2:

Given well-established sex differences in the expression of aggression, we expect men to score higher than women on physical and verbal aggression.

Prediction 3: Considering sex differences in the use of aggression within intrasexual competition, we expect the following sex-specific associations: 

a. We predict that the associations that both the core of the Dark Triad and psychopathy have with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger in men than in women, reflecting a greater reliance on direct, contest-based competition among men. 

b. We predict that the association between the core of the Dark Triad and hostility will be stronger in women than in men. Additionally, we expect positive associations between Machiavellianism and hostility in women but not in men—consistent with a greater reliance on indirect, scramble competition among women.

In addition to our primary predictions concerning sex as a moderator, we preregister a secondary prediction informed by evolutionary theory on intrasexual competition. Specifically, we will examine whether a short-term mating orientation (STMO) moderates the associations between the Dark Triad and aggression. If intrasexual competition is the driving mechanism between sexual differences, we predict that a higher STMO will strengthen these associations. This prediction is theoretically motivated but considered supplementary to our main specification.
table.datasets_used:
The dataset includes a total of 600 Spanish-speaking Chilean participants. The sample comprises university students (n = 316) and members of the general population (n = 284), recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory’s website. Participants were 353 women (M = 26.98 years, SD = 6.56) and 247 men (M = 24.98 years, SD = 5.68). Data collection took place at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo. The only exclusion criterion was being under 18 years of age.

The data were originally gathered as part of a previous project from one of the coauthors, where measures of trait aggression and Dark Triad traits served as control variables. For the present study, we will analyze these measures as primary outcomes of interest. Participants completed the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ) and the Short Dark Triad questionnaire (SD3), among a broader battery of instruments administered prior to the main experimental procedures. The dataset is cross-sectional, with all measures collected at a single time point.
table.data_availability: The dataset is not publicly available
table.data_access: The finalized dataset has been uploaded to this project as a private file and will be made public at the publishing phase.
table.access_date: The dataset was originally accessed in november 2024, at which time descriptive statistics and a confirmatory factor analysis were conducted. Since that point, the data have not been further analyzed.
table.data_collection_procedures:
Data were collected as part of a larger FONDECYT-funded project on aggression and cooperation conducted at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo. Participants were recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory’s website, as well as university mailing lists. Interested individuals completed an eligibility screening (no couples within the same group), and were scheduled into sessions of six participants each. Group composition was stratified by sex and parental status to create five predefined group types.

Upon arrival, participants completed a battery of self-report questionnaires (including the Short Dark Triad [SD3], the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire [BPAQ], the Multidimensional Sociosexual Orientation Inventory [SOI-M], and the Big Five Inventory [BFI]) before engaging in laboratory behavioral tasks (Point Subtraction Aggression Paradigm, Public Goods Game). Questionnaires were administered in Spanish in a controlled laboratory environment.

The sample is not nationally representative: it consists of university students and volunteers from the general population in central Chile who responded to online and university recruitment efforts. Participants received a payment related to transportation costs (fixed) and another associated with the decisions made in the economic games. Possible biases include self-selection and urban concentration. These factors should be kept in mind when interpreting generalizability.
table.manipulated_variables: Not applicable, this is an observational (correlational) study.
table.measured_variables:
Outcome (endogenous) variables (Aggression):

Aggression will be measured with the Spanish adaptation (Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014) of the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire (Buss & Perry, 1992; BPAQ; 29 items). Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = Extremely uncharacteristic of me to 5 = Extremely characteristic of me). The BPAQ produces four subscales, which will be modeled as endogenous latent variables. Following standard practice, covariances across endogenous aggression variables will be freely estimated.

- Physical Aggression (9 items; e.g., “Given enough provocation, I may hit another person”), α = .79.

- Verbal Aggression (5 items; e.g., “My friends say that I’m somewhat argumentative”). α = .69.

- Anger (7 items; e.g., “I have trouble controlling my temper”). α = .77.

- Hostility (8 items; e.g., “I sometimes feel that people are laughing at me behind my back”). α = .75.

Predictor (exogenous) variables (Dark Triad):

Dark Triad traits will be measured with the Spanish adaptation (Pineda et al., 2020) of the Short Dark Triad (Jones & Paulhus, 2014; SD3; 27 items), using 5-point Likert scales (1 = Strongly disagree to 5 = Strongly agree). The SD3 consists of three 9-item subscales:

- Machiavellianism (e.g., “You should wait for the right time to get back at people”), α = .74.

- Narcissism (e.g., “I know that I am special because everyone keeps telling me so”), α = .62.

- Psychopathy (e.g., “People who mess with me always regret it”), α = .63. Due to two psychopathy items with very low standardized loadings (λ < .10), we will conduct sensitivity analyses with and without these items.

- In addition, we will model a Dark Triad Core factor. A bifactor specification will be used: each item loads on a general Dark Core factor as well as its trait-specific factor (Machiavellianism, narcissism, or psychopathy). 

Following standard bifactor model practice, we will fix covariances between the Dark Core and the unique trait components to zero. We will test both a specification with zero and free covariances across the unique trait components as a robustness check for the Dark Core as the only source of shared variance among the Dark Triad (Jones & Figueredo, 2013).

Moderator:

- Sex: self-reported as male or female. This variable will be coded as a binary dummy (0 = female, 1 = male).

Control:

- Age: self-reported in years (continuous).

Secondary variables:

- Short Term Mating Orientation (Figueroa et al., 2025; SOI-M, 10 items; e.g., “I can easily imagine myself being comfortable and enjoying casual sex with different partners”). This measure is considered for the secondary prediction, not our main specification.

Residual covariances among items/indicators will be fixed to 0, consistent with standard CFA assumptions. Model fit will be evaluated using common indices available under each estimator (e.g., CFI, TLI, RMSEA, SRMR for ML/WLSMV; posterior predictive checks if Bayesian is needed). We will report all indices provided by the estimation method and evaluate fit holistically, considering conventional guidelines.

table.statistical_tests:
All preregistered analyses will be conducted using structural equation modeling (SEM). The SEM framework is chosen because it allows modeling latent constructs from multiple indicators (Bollen, 1989), and statistically separating the Dark Triad core using a bifactor structure (Rodriguez et al., 2016), as well as testing sex moderation through interaction terms.

Measurement model

* Aggression: Four latent factors from the Buss–Perry Aggression Questionnaire: Physical Aggression (9 items), Verbal Aggression (5 items), Anger (7 items), and Hostility (8 items).

* Dark Triad core: A general latent factor defined by the shared variance across Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy. Loads on every SD3 indicator.

* Unique/residual Dark Triad components: Three latent factors from the Short Dark Triad: Machiavellianism, Narcissism, and Psychopathy (9 items each). Unique variance after accounting for the Dark Triad core.

Structural models

* Model 1 (main effects and sex differences, prediction 1 and 2):
    * Physical Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex
    * Verbal Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex
    * Hostility ~ Dark Core + residual Narcissism
    * Anger ~ Dark Core

* Model 2 (sex moderation, prediction 3a and 3b): Adds sex × trait interaction terms:
    * Physical Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Psychopathy)
    * Verbal Aggression ~ Dark Core + residual Psychopathy + Sex + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Psychopathy)
    * Hostility ~ Dark Core + residual Narcissism + residual Machiavellianism + (Sex × Dark Core) + (Sex × residual Machiavellianism)
    * Anger ~ Dark Core (no moderation predicted)

In addition to conventional SEM estimates, we will compute trait-level total effects using a Variance-Weighted Latent Effect (VWLE) framework, which reformulates the total effect of a trait as a variance-share–weighted combination of its general (Dark Core) and trait-specific components. In practice, VWLE will be implemented as a non-linear test on model coefficients using the delta method (frequentist) or posterior transformations (Bayesian). The VWLE approach is an ongoing methodological development by the first author; a technical report describing the VWLE framework has been archived in the associated OSF project. table.inference_criteria: Effects will be evaluated with two-tailed tests at α = .05. If Bayesian estimation is needed, we will report 0.95 posterior credibility intervals.
table.assumption_violation_model_non_convergen:
Residual psychopathy factor:
Prior work (e.g., de Roos et al., 2017) and our own preliminary CFA with the SD3 indicate that the Dark Core explains nearly all of the variance in psychopathy (λ ≈ .98–.99). This suggests that the unique variance of psychopathy may be negligible once the Dark Core is partialled out. We preregister this as a test of equivalence between SD3 psychopathy and the Dark Core. If the bifactor model fails to converge, or if the residual psychopathy factor is empirically indistinguishable (e.g., all item loadings near zero), we will interpret this as evidence that SD3 psychopathy is fully represented by the Dark Core. In this case, we will remove the residual psychopathy factor from the model and treat psychopathy as equivalent to the Dark Core in subsequent structural analyses.

Distributional assumptions:
If multivariate normality assumptions are violated, models will be estimated using polychoric correlations with robust SEM estimators (e.g., WLSMV) and, where appropriate, ordinal SEM (GSEM).

Generalized non-convergence:
If models fail to converge more broadly, we will re-estimate using Bayesian SEM with weakly informative priors.

Specific bootstrap variants will be selected based on the inferential target and reported transparently.

Cross-validation: We will report within-sample cross-validation (e.g., k-fold) for overall model fit as a descriptive check of replicability.

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 5 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (5). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 14 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. text.text: Although the Dark Triad (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) has been consistently linked to aggressive behaviors such as bullying and violence, two important questions about these associations remain unresolved.
First, little is known about how they differ between women and men.
Second, it remains unclear how factor overlap affects their substantive interpretation.
Drawing on evolutionary accounts of intrasexual competition, we predict stronger associations with physical and verbal aggression in men and hostility in women.
We test these predictions on Short Dark Triad and Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire data from 600 Chilean adults, using bifactor (S-1) structural equation modeling.
We find that Machiavellianism predicts all aggression outcomes, psychopathy-specific variance positively predicts physical aggression, and narcissism-specific variance negatively predicts hostility.
Sex differences in aggression overlap with sex differences in aversive traits, but none of the Dark Triad-aggression associations consistently differ by sex.
By introducing the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE), we provide the first substantive translation of these bifactor associations.

VWLE clarifies how reference facet and trait-specific associations reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism, making the implications of residual coefficients explicit.
A defining feature of individuals high in Dark Triad traits (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) is their heightened propensity for aggressive behavior (Furnham et al., 2013).
text.formatted: A defining feature of individuals high in Dark Triad traits (i.e., psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and narcissism) is their heightened propensity for aggressive behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Furnham et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: These traits have been linked to various forms of aggression, including bullying (Baughman et al., 2012; van Geel et al., 2017), support for politically motivated violence (Nai & Young, 2024), and criminal behavior (Brugués & Caparrós, 2022; Hampejs et al., 2025).
text.formatted: These traits have been linked to various forms of aggression, including bullying <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Baughman et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">van Geel et al., 2017)</ref>, support for politically motivated violence <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Nai & Young, 2024)</ref>, and criminal behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Brugués & Caparrós, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Hampejs et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, these investigations have rarely considered sex differences.

A substantial body of evidence suggests that men and women differ in the expression of aggression (Archer, 2004), with these differences often attributed to evolutionary pressures such as sexual selection (Archer, 2009).
text.formatted: A substantial body of evidence suggests that men and women differ in the expression of aggression <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Archer, 2004)</ref>, with these differences often attributed to evolutionary pressures such as sexual selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Archer, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This raises the possibility that men and women high in aversive personality traits may express distinct aggressive strategies in pursuit of their goals, but the literature has yet to elucidate this relationship.
Moreover, previous research has not yet resolved how overlap among Dark Triad traits affects the substantive interpretation of their relationships with aggression.

We examine whether sex moderates the relationship between Dark Triad traits and dispositional aggression, and introduce the variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE) to clarify the interpretation of these associations in the presence of factor overlap.

Sexual selection theory explains the evolution of traits that enhance mating success through two primary mechanisms: intersexual selection and intrasexual competition, whereby individuals compete with same-sex rivals for access to potential mates (D. M. Buss, 1989; D. M. Buss & Schmitt, 2019; Darwin, 1871; Puts, 2016).

text.text: In humans, females are argued to have faced evolutionary pressures associated with greater fitness costs from physical aggression (Campbell, 1999).

text.text: In contrast, males tend to exhibit greater variability in reproductive success (Brown et al., 2009), which fosters strategies that emphasize direct, often aggressive, competition for mates, including dominance displays and physical confrontations (Archer, 2009; Campbell, 2006).

text.text: Therefore, sex differences are expected to shape both the prevalence and form of aggressive behavior.
Aggression is a multifaceted construct encompassing instrumental, affective, and cognitive components.
The instrumental component 1 involves the intentional delivery of harm to others and can be expressed in both verbal and physical forms.
The affective component centers on the emotional experience of anger that prepares the individual for aggressive action.
The cognitive component, often referred to as hostility, includes negative thoughts and beliefs that motivate aggressive behavior (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992).
text.formatted: The cognitive component, often referred to as hostility, includes negative thoughts and beliefs that motivate aggressive behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Aggression can be expressed through both direct and indirect forms.

Direct aggression entails overt acts such as physical violence or verbal attacks, whereas indirect aggression involves covert strategies, such as manipulating others to harm the target (Björkqvist et al., 1992).
text.formatted: Direct aggression entails overt acts such as physical violence or verbal attacks, whereas indirect aggression involves covert strategies, such as manipulating others to harm the target <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Björkqvist et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: From an evolutionary perspective, aggression is broadly defined as behavior aimed at inflicting costs on others, with its role in intrasexual competition among its most salient functions (D. M. Buss & Shackelford, 1997).
text.formatted: From an evolutionary perspective, aggression is broadly defined as behavior aimed at inflicting costs on others, with its role in intrasexual competition among its most salient functions (D. M. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Buss & Shackelford, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this evolutionary function, research has established sex differences in preferred forms of aggression.
Men display more direct and riskier forms of aggressive behavior, a finding that is well-documented across studies (Daly & Wilson, 1990 , 2001).

text.text: (1) Based on prior findings, we predict that the shared variance of the Dark Triad (i.e., Dark Core) will be positively associated with all components of aggression in both men and women.

In addition, psychopathy is expected to exhibit unique positive associations with physical and verbal aggression, whereas narcissism is anticipated to show a unique negative association with hostility.
(2) Given well-established sex differences in the expression of aggression, we expect men to score higher than women on physical and verbal aggression.

(3) Considering sex differences in the use of aggression within intrasexual competition, we expect the following sex-specific associations: (a) The associations of both the shared variance and psychopathy with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger in men than in women, reflecting a greater reliance on direct, contest-based competition among men. (b) The association between the shared variance and hostility will be stronger in women than in men.
Additionally, Machiavellianism will be positively associated with hostility in women but not in men, consistent with a greater reliance on indirect, scramble competition among women.

Evaluating the associations of the Dark Triad with external outcomes such as aggression leads to an open methodological challenge: high intercorrelations between traits make it difficult to disentangle their unique contributions.
This challenge has generated debate over appropriate statistical approaches and theoretical interpretations (Furnham et al., 2014; Sleep et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This challenge has generated debate over appropriate statistical approaches and theoretical interpretations <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Furnham et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Sleep et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One widely adopted solution has been to isolate the shared variance using bifactor models (McLarnon & Tarraf, 2017) and analyze it separately from the unique components of each trait.
text.formatted: One widely adopted solution has been to isolate the shared variance using bifactor models <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(McLarnon & Tarraf, 2017)</ref> and analyze it separately from the unique components of each trait.

text.text: However, this approach introduces a secondary challenge.

Namely, bifactor models explicitly residualize traits relative to one another, raising concerns about whether their results can be interpreted as associations involving the original constructs (Hoyle et al., 2023; Miller et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Namely, bifactor models explicitly residualize traits relative to one another, raising concerns about whether their results can be interpreted as associations involving the original constructs <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hoyle et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Miller et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, effects of residual components may not hold at the first-order level due to suppressionfoot_2 , and may imply associations that are hard to justify substantively (Sleep et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In particular, effects of residual components may not hold at the first-order level due to suppression<ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">foot_2</ref> , and may imply associations that are hard to justify substantively <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Sleep et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The direct structural interpretation of bifactor residual coefficients is semi-partial (Eid et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The direct structural interpretation of bifactor residual coefficients is semi-partial <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Eid et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For example, in an S -1 model with Machiavellianism as the reference facet, the psychopathy coefficient indicates how aggression varies with psychopathy above or below the level expected from a person's Machiavellianism (Eid et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For example, in an S -1 model with Machiavellianism as the reference facet, the psychopathy coefficient indicates how aggression varies with psychopathy above or below the level expected from a person's Machiavellianism <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Eid et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet conditioning at the measurement stage leaves the magnitudes of those expectations and departures, and thus the structure against which coefficients are interpreted, implicit.
To narrow this gap, we present a pilot implementation of the VWLE, a technique that consolidates this information for substantive interpretation.
VWLE is the estimand that specifically targets conceptual overlap by weighting shared and residual component contributions to reconstruct a trait's first-order association with an outcome.

In this study, we (1) examine whether the relationships between the Dark Triad and aggression differ between women and men, and (2) use the VWLE to illustrate how factor overlap can affect the substantive conclusions drawn for these relationships.
>Materials and methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and methods</head>

text.text: The study includes a total of 600 Chilean participants, all of whom are Spanish-speaking.
The sample is composed of university students (n = 316) and members of the general population (n = 284), recruited through public announcements on social networks and the laboratory's website.
The sample consists of 353 women (M = 26.98, SD = 6.56, range = 18-47 years) and 247 men (M = 24.98, SD = 5.68, range = 18-44 years).
The data were collected at the Laboratorio de Comportamiento Animal y Humano (LABCAH), Universidad del Desarrollo.
No exclusion criteria were specified aside from being at least 18 years of age.
>Measurements
text.formatted: <head n="2.2." >Measurements</head>

text.text: Dispositional aggression is measured with a Spanish-validated (Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014) version of the Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ -A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992).
text.formatted: Dispositional aggression is measured with a Spanish-validated <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Valdivia-Peralta et al., 2014)</ref> version of the Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire (BPAQ -A. H. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Buss & Perry, 1992)</ref>.

text.text: This questionnaire is a widely used self-report measure evaluating individual differences in aggression across four dimensions: Physical Aggression (e.g., "Given enough provocation, I may hit another person"), Verbal Aggression (e.g., "My friends say that I'm somewhat argumentative"), Hostility ("I sometimes feel that people are laughing at me behind my back"), and Anger (e.g., "I have trouble controlling my temper").
The BPAQ comprises 29 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 ("Extremely uncharacteristic of me") to 5 ("Extremely characteristic of me") (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992).

text.text: Dark Triad personality traits are measured with a Spanish-validated (Pineda et al., 2020) version of the Short Dark Triad questionnaire (SD3 -D. N. Jones & Paulhus, 2014), which assesses Machiavellianism (e.g., "You should wait for the right time to get back at people"), psychopathy (e.g., "People who mess with me always regret it") and narcissism (e.g., "I know that I am special because everyone keeps telling me so").

We use structural equation modeling (SEM) to evaluate our predictions.
We start by testing for measurement invariance between sexes in each questionnaire to assess whether the constructs are measured comparably in women and men.

We then use lasso regularized multigroup (Huang, 2018) confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) to identify non-invariant items for our primary partial-scalar-invariant measurement specifications (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).

All predictions involving the shared variance of the scale (i.e., Dark Core) are indirectly assessed by the inclusion of the reference facet carrying it.

The second model adds the confirmatory interactions for Prediction 3a-that the associations of the reference facet and psychopathy with physical and verbal aggression will be stronger among men-and Prediction 3b-that the associations of the reference facet with hostility will be stronger among women.
Moderation involving a separate Machiavellianism-specific component cannot be assessed in this parameterization.
All confirmatory models control for age and freely estimate residual covariances among the aggression outcomes.
Prediction 2-that men will report greater physical and verbal aggression-is evaluated using unconditional sex differences.
Subsequent exploratory models include all interactions between the Dark Triad components and sex to situate the focal effects within the broader pattern of associations.
Measurement and structural models are estimated using robust maximum likelihood.
Full-sample analyses use 500 MI draws, with asymptotic inference based on pooling within-and between-imputation variance according to Rubin's (1987) total variance rule.

We further present the pilot implementation of the VWLE-an ongoing methodological development by the first author-which translates partial effects from the reducedform bifactor model to the first-order construct level for substantive interpretation (see Appendix E for derivation and implementation details).
For non-reference traits, the implemented oblique-least-squares VWLE releases conditioning on the reference facet while retaining adjustment for sibling-specific components and covariates.
VWLE estimates are presented descriptively and are not used for confirmatory inference.

text.text: VWLE estimates translate these component-level coefficients into the original Dark Triad coordinates.
The reference Machiavellianism and specific-component associations reinforce one another when their directions align, but cancel one another when their signs oppose.
Narcissism provides the clearest example: its negative specific association with hostility is largely offset by its positive reference contribution, yielding a negligible first-order association.

text.text: It reveals that psychopathy parallels the broad pattern observed for the reference Machiavellianism, with moderate to large associations with hostility (η² semi = .071) and verbal aggression (η² semi = .152), and very large associations with physical aggression (η² semi = .248) and anger (η² semi = .242).

In the jointly estimated system, excluding psychopathy from an equation leaves psychopathy-related variation in its residual, which may attenuate its estimated associations elsewhere through the correlated residuals.
This is especially relevant to the verbal aggression estimate, which changes dramatically relative to the confirmatory specification.
Expanding the conditioning set also enhances the scores of women relative to men even further, with meaningful changes to verbal aggression (η² semi = .014) and anger estimates (η² semi = .125).

text.text: Descriptively, psychopathy generally shows the strongest associations across aggression outcomes, followed by Machiavellianism, which matches it in hostility.
Even accounting for its shared-variance component, the associations of narcissism with trait aggression are very small.
We examine how Dark Triad traits relate to different forms of dispositional aggression in women and men.

Our analyses reveal broad support for Prediction 1: the reference facet of the Dark Triad is positively associated with all aggression outcomes, psychopathy has a unique positive association with physical aggression, and narcissism has a unique negative association with hostility.
Psychopathy also shows the expected unique association with verbal aggression, but only once its associations across all correlated aggression outcomes are appropriately represented.

Prediction 2 receives partial support: we find sex differences in raw aggression scores for physical and verbal aggression in favor of men, but only the difference in physical aggression remains supported after accounting for measurement non-invariance.
Finally, Prediction 3 receives no support: we do not find larger associations with the Dark Triad in physical and verbal aggression for men, nor in hostility for women.
Sex differences involving a Machiavellianism-specific component are not evaluated.

In light of Machiavellianism's small facet-specific variance in the higher-order representation (see Table A6), its associations with aggression outcomes support the view that the antagonistic features shared across Dark Triad traits (Paulhus & Williams, 2002) represent a general disposition toward aggression (D. N. Jones & Neria, 2015).

text.text: Psychopathy nevertheless contributes beyond the reference facet.

These unique associations may be explained by psychopathy's impulsive tendencies (Paulhus & Williams, 2002), which seem not only to facilitate the behavioral expression of aggression (Bresin, 2019) but also enhance its cognitive and affective components.

text.text: The particularly strong association of psychopathy with anger deserves special attention.

As Archer and Webb (2006) note, BPAQ anger items overlap with direct measures of impulsiveness, suggesting that part of the association of psychopathy with anger may reflect common item content rather than an underlying structural relationship.

text.text: Moreover, although narcissistic individuals respond aggressively when ego-threatened (Krizan & Johar, 2015; Stucke & Sporer, 2002), these context-dependent reactions may not be fully captured by trait-level measures.

text.text: Thus, narcissism's weaker association with dispositional aggression may reflect the failure of such assessments to account for situational triggers.

At the unconditional level, the raw observed sex differences across BPAQ dimensions broadly align with previous findings: men score substantially higher in physical aggression, slightly higher in verbal aggression, and do not consistently differ from women in hostility (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Jain et al., 2023).

text.text: Moreover, our data suggest that raw differences in verbal aggression may be driven by measurement non-invariance.
The remaining difference in physical aggression is consistent with sexual-selection accounts emphasizing greater male engagement in direct intrasexual competition (Puts et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The remaining difference in physical aggression is consistent with sexual-selection accounts emphasizing greater male engagement in direct intrasexual competition <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">(Puts et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The general shift of the expected scores in favor of women after conditioning on the Dark Triad suggests that unconditional differences partly overlap with sex differences in aversive traits.
However, the moderation results qualify an interpretation of the male-Dark Triad overlap as evidence that aversive traits specifically channel male contest competition into aggressive dispositions.

If interpreted through contest competition, this pattern implies a mechanism that may also operate among women, with male predominance driven mainly by differences in the distribution of Dark Triad scores between sexes.
Conditional differences in hostility, verbal aggression and anger also raise questions about the interpretation of men as more dispositionally aggressive.
Men's higher Dark Triad scores should, by themselves, predict greater scores across these subscales.
Yet women generally report equivalent levels of hostility (A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992; Jain et al., 2023) and, in this case, equivalent levels of verbal aggression and higher levels of anger.
text.formatted: Yet women generally report equivalent levels of hostility <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(A. H. Buss & Perry, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Jain et al., 2023)</ref> and, in this case, equivalent levels of verbal aggression and higher levels of anger.

text.text: If cognitive-and possibly affective-aggressive dispositions can be interpreted as reflecting a tendency toward indirect forms of intrasexual competition, then we are led to a symmetric interpretation: aversive traits similarly enhance direct and indirect forms of intrasexual competition.
Women's higher baseline levels of the latter then suggest a complementary mechanism that offsets their lower average levels of Dark Triad traits, although this remains an open research question.

Our original account located sex differentiation in the expression of aversive traits, where sexual selection was expected to strengthen the translation of these traits into direct aggression among men and into hostility among women.
The results instead suggest this differentiation may be upstream.

A revised interpretation under the framework of intrasexual competition may be that selection operates at the frequency (Wilson, 1994) at which these traits emerge within sexes, rather than on how they implement competitive strategies.
text.formatted: A revised interpretation under the framework of intrasexual competition may be that selection operates at the frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Wilson, 1994)</ref> at which these traits emerge within sexes, rather than on how they implement competitive strategies.

text.text: We note that this interpretation remains tentative, as the current design cannot rule out competing explanations for the observed pattern.
Considerable debate in the Dark Triad literature concerns how best to study the associations of these strongly overlapping traits with external outcomes (Furnham et al., 2014; Sleep et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Considerable debate in the Dark Triad literature concerns how best to study the associations of these strongly overlapping traits with external outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Furnham et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Sleep et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One widely adopted approach invokes a common Dark Core underlying this overlap (D. N. Jones & Figueredo, 2013; Vize et al., 2020) and uses bifactor models to distinguish associations attributable to the general component from those unique to each trait.
text.formatted: One widely adopted approach invokes a common Dark Core underlying this overlap (D. N. <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Jones & Figueredo, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Vize et al., 2020)</ref> and uses bifactor models to distinguish associations attributable to the general component from those unique to each trait.

text.text: However, bifactor models leave the structure against which residual coefficients are interpreted implicit.
The oblique VWLE expresses a trait's first-order association while holding only specific sibling components and non-sibling variables fixed.
It therefore extends the first-order interpretation directly available for the reference facet in an S -1 model to non-reference traitsfoot_4 .
text.formatted: It therefore extends the first-order interpretation directly available for the reference facet in an S -1 model to non-reference traits<ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">foot_4</ref> .

text.text: For psychopathy, this means relaxing conditioning on the Machiavellianism reference while retaining adjustment for the narcissism-specific component.
In the present study, this translation shows how the reference facet and trait-specific associations combine: they reinforce one another for psychopathy but largely cancel out for narcissism.
The translations are nontrivial in magnitude.
For hostility, a substantial unique effect of psychopathy produces a barely noticeable difference between psychopathy and the reference Machiavellianism at the first-order level.
By contrast, the unique associations involving psychopathy markedly differentiate first-order psychopathy from Machiavellianism in the other equations.
Thus, VWLE may bridge the gap between theory and estimation by making the substantive implications of residual coefficients explicit.
Several limitations qualify these results.
Most importantly, the BPAQ does not provide a dedicated measure of indirect aggression, and our conclusions rely on hostility as an empirically motivated approximation (Archer & Webb, 2006).
text.formatted: Most importantly, the BPAQ does not provide a dedicated measure of indirect aggression, and our conclusions rely on hostility as an empirically motivated approximation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Archer & Webb, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Both the operationalization of predictions and the interpretations concerning intrasexual competition should therefore be regarded as suggestive.
Future studies should employ dedicated measures of both direct and indirect aggression, and also distinguish aggression toward same-sex versus other-sex targets explicitly.

Second, the SD3 provides relatively narrow measurements of multidimensional traits, while the modest fit and reliability of some of its factors further limit construct coverage and precision-a finding that resonates with the wider literature regarding the scale's psychometric properties (Knitter et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Second, the SD3 provides relatively narrow measurements of multidimensional traits, while the modest fit and reliability of some of its factors further limit construct coverage and precision-a finding that resonates with the wider literature regarding the scale's psychometric properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Knitter et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: More comprehensive assessments of the Dark Triad traits are therefore needed.

Relatedly, meaningful absolute estimates and asymptotic inference do not allow us to conclusively rule out sex differences opposite to the predicted direction for physical and verbal aggression on psychopathy (see Table B2).
text.formatted: Relatedly, meaningful absolute estimates and asymptotic inference do not allow us to conclusively rule out sex differences opposite to the predicted direction for physical and verbal aggression on psychopathy (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">B2</ref>).

text.text: Better measurements may help clarify this question.
Finally, because the findings rely on cross-sectional self-reports of dispositions, their extension to competitive and aggressive behavior in real-world settings remains to be examined.
VWLE should likewise be regarded as a descriptive pilot implementation.
Although the estimator is supported by a mathematical proof and preliminary empirical validation (see Table E1), its broader statistical properties remain to be established.
text.formatted: Although the estimator is supported by a mathematical proof and preliminary empirical validation (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">E1</ref>), its broader statistical properties remain to be established.

text.text: The bootstrap standard errors give a provisional indication of sampling variability, but analytic standard errors have not yet been derived.
Exactness of the first-order reconstruction under the current feasible least-squares implementation assumes orthogonality between direct-general and specific factor loadings (see Section E.3).
Our findings reproduce a broad pattern of associations consistently reported in the Dark Triad and aggression literature and suggest that it may hold for both women and men.
By introducing the VWLE, we provide the first substantive translation of this component-level pattern into associations involving the original traits.
The present study therefore contributes to the consolidation of the field's main empirical findings within a common substantive framework.
The bifactor model answers how shared and specific components from a set of overlapping factors relate to an outcome.
VWLE then answers what those component-level associations imply for the factors themselves.

text.text: Table A4.
Blockwise multigroup Aggression (BPAQ) and Dark Triad (SD3) measurement model fit metrics across women and men.
Dark Triad measurement uses a bifactor (S -1) with Machiavellianism as the reference facet.

The configural model specifies the same factor structure with loadings and item intercepts freely estimated across groups; the metric model constrains factor loadings to equality across groups; the scalar model additionally constrains item intercepts; the partial model frees constraints on the item intercepts whose differences between groups show the largest contributions to the likelihood function under regularization.

BPAQ = Buss and Perry Aggression Questionnaire; SD3 = Short Dark Triad; CFI = robust comparative fit index; RMSEA = robust root mean square error of approximation; SRMR = standardized root mean square residual.

Robust CFI values were calculated using a common independence model with item means and variances constrained equal across groups. ∆ denotes the current model's value minus the preceding model's value.
Changes in the partial model are expressed with respect to the metric model.
Models were estimated using robust maximum likelihood.
Constraining factor loadings to equality across women and men produces negligible changes in fit in the SD3 and small changes in the BPAQ, broadly supporting metric invariance.

Additional equality constraints on item intercepts yield mixed evidence for scalar invariance: robust CFI decreases by .038 for the BPAQ and .028 for the SD3, whereas RMSEA and SRMR increase only slightly (.006 for both indices in the BPAQ and .003 and .004 for the SD3, respectively).
A partial scalar invariance specification further frees item intercepts whose difference between groups show the largest contributions to the likelihood function.
To identify non-invariant item intercepts, we use lasso regularized CFA with 10-fold cross-validation to rank candidate intercept differences.
Following this ranking, we fit successive partial scalar-invariant models, freeing one additional item intercept at each step.
In each model, we test the between-group differences in all freed intercepts.
We retain the specification immediately preceding the first model in which any freed intercept difference has an absolute z statistic below 1.96, the critical value for a two-tailed test at α = .05.
All remaining item intercepts remain constrained to equality across groups.
For the BPAQ, following this procedure frees 7 out of the 29 items (3 out of 9 for physical aggression, 1 out of 5 for verbal aggression, 2 out of 8 for hostility, and 1 out of 7 for anger).
For the SD3, the procedure frees 4 out of the 27 items (3 out of 9 for narcissism and 1 out of 9 for psychopathy).
Across scales, the partial specifications are in line with conventional guidelines.

To assess whether the linear treatment of ordinal item responses may contribute to modest configural fit, we re-estimate the configural measurement models using diagonally weighted least squares (DWLS), with robust standard errors and a mean-and variance-adjusted test statistic.
All items are treated as ordered categorical variables.
Robust CFI values are calculated using a common independence baseline with item thresholds constrained equal across groups.

Neither ordinal specification improves fit over its linear counterpart, giving worse absolute metrics across fit indices (BPAQ: CFI = .713, RMSEA = .095, SRMR = .078; SD3: CFI = .662, RMSEA = .084, SRMR = .074).

To address concerns over modest measurement fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999) influencing structural analyses, we construct an alternative measurement specification relaxing some residual covariance constraints.

text.text: Using lasso regularization, we identify and freely estimate the residual covariances with the largest contributions to model likelihood: 12 of 406 possible covariances for the BPAQ and 10 of 351 for the SD3.

However, if ξ (1) has a nested or overlapping factor structure, the direct first-order estimands will not correspond, in general, to the target first-order effects.

By the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem (FWL -Frisch & Waugh, 1933; Lovell, 1963), conditioning on sibling variables distributes the effect of the general component across the overlapping block, making the effects for the ξ (1) j ∈ ξ (1) defined with respect to a residual coordinate composed of their specific component plus the part of the general factor not linearly recovered by the remaining sibling factors.

text.text: The variance-weighted latent effect (VWLE) is the model-implied estimand that reconstructs first-order effects from a bifactor model by weighting general and specific component effects according to the variance structure implied by the measurement model.
The oblique or type-two VWLE implemented in this article is the reduced-form best linear predictor that relaxes conditioning on a latent block's overlapping general factor.

Then, for each target facet in the original saturated specification, we fit an auxiliary model jointly replacing the S -1 reference regressor, the target specific component, and their component-by-sex terms with the reconstructed first-order regressor and its interaction with sex.

The results confirm the expected behavior of the oblique VWLE estimator, yielding numerically equivalent point estimates for both main and interaction effects from a single reference-model fit and multiple auxiliary fits using direct parametrizations of the corresponding oblique first-order effects.

Under the current stratified two-stage framework (von Hippel, 2009), VWLE estimates combine information from the multigroup measurement model and the pooled structural model, assuming compatibility of the stratified factor loadings and bifactor orthogonality restrictions with the pooled structural covariance.
However, metric invariance supports common factor loadings, and within-sex bifactor orthogonality carries over to the sex-adjusted pooled covariance by the law of total covariance.
